passage:
Dear Thomas,
I owe you an honest note. Remember the billing sheet crash in March? I patched it at midnight with a hidden column that copied numbers by hand, and told you I would rebuild it properly after the audit. I meant it. Then came the new client, the festival rush, the team's leave. Seven months later the hidden column is still there, and three new people have built reports on top of it. Last week it broke on the first day of the month and we spent two days finding out why. I felt sick, because I knew exactly which shortcut it was. From next week I am blocking Friday afternoons to replace it, and I would like you to check my plan.
Vinita

qa.q: How long had the hidden column stayed after the March patch?
qa.a: It had stayed for seven months.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when the sheet broke?
qa.a: Sick and guilty, knowing exactly which shortcut had caused it.

qa.q: What does Vinita plan to do about it?
qa.a: Block Friday afternoons to replace the patch and ask Thomas to check the plan.

qa.q: How might the three new people have been affected?
qa.a: They built reports on a fragile patch they did not know about, and lost two days when it broke.

grounding: Shows a worker who patched something in a hurry, promised a proper fix later, and let the patch become permanent.

passage: Uday, you asked about my worst shortcut, and it is tiny, which is the scary part. I'm Sharmila, and two years ago the kitchen's order printer kept failing at the Friday rush. I set a timer to restart it every ten minutes and taped a note to the wall: "temporary, fix properly Monday." Monday came and we were busy. So did the next Monday. Now the timer has been running two years, every new cook learns the ritual, nobody knows why, and last month when the timer failed the whole line stopped for an hour. Fixing it properly took forty minutes. I had spent countless hours working around it.

qa.q: How often did the timer restart the order printer?
qa.a: The timer restarted the printer every ten minutes.

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel looking back at the shortcut?
qa.a: Regretful and a little alarmed, calling it the scary part that something so small lasted so long.

qa.q: What could Sharmila have done on the first Monday?
qa.a: Set aside forty minutes to fix it properly, since that is all the fix took in the end.

qa.q: How might a new cook see the timer ritual?
qa.a: As a puzzling routine to follow without knowing why, since nobody can explain it.

grounding: Shows a worker whose hurried patch, promised to be fixed later, becomes a permanent burden.
